You are a debugging assistant. You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure, and several recent issue reports that have been pre-filtered by an external semantic retrieval model (SBERT) to be the most relevant to this failure among recent reports.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– likely-relevant recent bug reports,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.
Treat "likely-relevant recent bug reports" as secondary evidence: they may or may not be relevant. Use them only if they help; otherwise, you may ignore them.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

Diagnosis:
The failing test case `workaroundForBrokenTimeHeader` tries to read an AIX native tar file containing symbolic links using the `TarArchiveInputStream`. The test expects to correctly read the symbolic link and its zero epoch modification date but the current bug report indicates an IOException is thrown due to an "Error detected parsing the header" at line 201 in `TarArchiveInputStream.getNextTarEntry()`.

From the code, `getNextTarEntry()` reads the next tar entry header bytes and constructs a `TarArchiveEntry` by parsing the header. The construction of `TarArchiveEntry` calls `parseTarHeader(byte[])` which reads various fields from the header, including file size, uid, gid, etc. These fields are parsed using `TarUtils.parseOctalOrBinary()`. This method can parse values encoded either as octal ASCII or as binary. It checks if the highest bit of the first byte is set to distinguish binary format, then parses the binary number as a signed long.

The problem likely arises because `TarUtils.parseOctalOrBinary()` expects certain length fields (like uid, gid) to contain a 12-byte sequence for parsing octal or binary data, but the AIX native tar header or the symlink header produces some values that do not conform, possibly causing `parseOctalOrBinary` to throw an IllegalArgumentException wrapped as IOException.

Recent similar reports mention `TarUtils.formatLongOctalOrBinaryBytes()` assuming fixed size fields, and a report indicating `TarArchiveInputStream` throws IllegalArgumentException on corrupt files (which is seen here), hinting that this method is sensitive to unexpected field lengths or encodings.

The test expects a symbolic link with a last modified date of the epoch (new Date(0)), which hints at the time field possibly being corrupted or encoded in a way not correctly handled by the current parser.

In summary, the root cause is that `TarArchiveInputStream.getNextTarEntry()` fails to parse tar headers created by AIX native tar for symlinks due to incompatibilities or unexpected binary encoding in the header fields, causing `TarUtils.parseOctalOrBinary` to throw an exception.

This explains why the test fails with an IOException related to parsing headers, and why symbolic link entries specifically from AIX tar files cannot be read.

The fix likely requires making the header parsing in `TarUtils.parseOctalOrBinary` and possibly `TarArchiveEntry.parseTarHeader` more robust for AIX tar quirks, or adding special handling for those cases in `TarArchiveInputStream.getNextTarEntry`.

Thus the bug occurred due to insufficient parsing flexibility or validation for AIX native tar header binary fields in `TarUtils.parseOctalOrBinary` used by `TarArchiveEntry` construction in `TarArchiveInputStream`.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
